newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani cement maker groans under tax burden.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani cement maker groans under tax burden.

text.p: The head of leading Pakistani cement manufacturer Maple Leaf Cement Factory Ltd has urged the government to act against unfair taxes which he said were strangling the cement sector.

Tariq Saigol, whose Kohinoor Rawalpindi group owns Maple Leaf Cement, said his company, along with the rest of the sector, has been hard-hit by debilitating taxes, sagging prices, sluggish demand and overcapacity.

In an interview with Reuters, he urged the caretaker government to reduce the industry's production costs, slash taxes and remove what he called politically motivated tax breaks for new cement plants in North West Frontier Province.

"The cement sector was unfortunately given stepmotherly treatment by the previous government," said Saigol, who is respected on both sides of Pakistan's political divide as an eloquent spokesman for the business lobby.
"For the cement industry, government intervention is necessary," Saigol said.
His group, among Pakistan's largest, also has direct interests in power generation and textiles.
Maple Leaf Cement's after-tax profit fell to about 141 million rupees ($3.5 million) in 1995/96 (July-June) from 217 million rupees in 1994/95.
"Our profits declined because selling prices came down, demand was slack and the availability of cement from new plants increased," Saigol said.
Production costs have rocketed as the price of furnace oil -- the most important cost factor in cement production -- has doubled in a year, he said.
Taxes have also soared, with a 35 percent excise duty charged on the ex-factory price of cement and an 18 percent sales tax on the retail price, making for combined taxes of nearly 55 percent.
Saigol said the former government of Benazir Bhutto had exempted new cement plants in North West Frontier Province from sales tax, distorting prices and competition.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule. He named a caretaker cabinet to oversee elections on February 3.
Mohammed Hanif, chairman of the coordination committee of the All Pakistan Cement Manufacturers' Association, last month demanded an end to the exemptions.

"The regional disparity in levying the sales tax is not only unfair for a level playing field to all; it is also against the government's avowed goal of weeding out exemptions," Hanif wrote to Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid.
"The original exemption was granted as a political favour and must be withdrawn so as not to create unfair competition and loss of government revenue," the letter said.

Brokerage researchers forecast that Pakistan's cement industry will be churning out a surplus of 3.56 million tonnes by the end of 1997, when they say supply will total 16.47 million tonnes against demand of 12.91 million tonnes.

Nevertheless, Saigol is going ahead with a new plant based on dry-process technology with a capacity of one million tonnes a year in collaboration with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the private lending arm of the World Bank.
The IFC has provided $80 million to Maple Leaf in equity and loans to set up the new seven billion rupee unit.
Maple Leaf's annual capacity, now 471,000 tonnes of grey cement and 30,000 tonnes of white cement, will reach 1.5 million tonnes when the new plant comes on stream in September 1997.
Saigol said the decision to invest in the new unit was taken because the old plant, bought from the state in 1992, used highly fuel-inefficient wet-process technology.
"I knew that ultimately I would have to go in for a new unit, otherwise the company would have collapsed," he said.
"But we had hoped that buoyant demand for cement would allow us to keep running the wet-process kilns for eight to 10 years more."
Saigol said Pakistan's existing per capita use of cement was 70 kg a year, well below the 120 kg average in similar-income countries. "It means there is suppressed demand," he added.
"If there was a possibility that the economy could be revived again and if growth becomes buoyant, than I feel that this capacity will be absorbed very quickly," Saigol said.
